passages.happening:
‘This is the vision of Obadiah’ (verse 1), the word of the Lord GOD about Edom. A messenger has gone out among the nations calling them to battle against her. ‘Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you will be deeply despised’ (verse 2).

‘The pride of your heart has deceived you, O dwellers in the clefts of the rocks whose habitation is the heights’ (verse 3), who say in their hearts that no one can bring them down. ‘Though you soar like the eagle and make your nest among the stars, even from there I will bring you down,’ declares the LORD (verse 4).

Thieves take only what they want, and grape pickers leave a little behind, but Esau will be stripped bare and his hidden treasures searched out (verses 5-6). His allies will drive him to the border, and those who eat his bread will set a trap for him (verse 7). On that day God will destroy the wise men of Edom, and the warriors of Teman will be terrified (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, in high, rocky country whose towns were hard to attack. Its people descended from Esau. David subdued Edom, but it broke free of Judah in the ninth century, and the two peoples fought on and off for generations. Its confidence came from its geography. The word for rock in verse 3 is sela, which was also the name of an Edomite stronghold; some have linked it with the later city of Petra, though that is uncertain.

Edom was also famous for wisdom. Teman, one of its districts, was praised for its wise men, and Eliphaz, one of Job's friends, was a Temanite. Those who eat your bread were allies bound by a shared meal, a sign of covenant loyalty. Edom will be betrayed by its own friends.

Much of these verses closely matches Jeremiah's word against Edom, which suggests that one prophet used the other or both drew on an older oracle. The pictures are of height brought low and of plunder so complete that nothing is left.
passages.later: Jeremiah speaks almost the same words: ‘Though you elevate your nest like the eagle, even from there I will bring you down’ (Jeremiah 49:16). Teman's wisdom is named in Jeremiah 49:7, and Eliphaz was a Temanite (Job 2:11).
passages.asks: Edom trusted its height, its wisdom and its friends. Ask what makes you feel out of reach. And ask what pride in your own heart has been deceiving you.

passages.happening:
‘Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame and cut off forever’ (verse 10). On the day strangers carried off Jacob's wealth and foreigners entered his gate and cast lots for Jerusalem, Edom stood aloof, ‘you were just like one of them’ (verse 11).

Then the prophet speaks as if he stood beside Edom on that day. It should not have gloated over its brother's misfortune, or rejoiced over Judah's destruction, or boasted in their distress (verse 12). It should not have entered the gate of God's people, gloated over their affliction or looted their wealth (verse 13). ‘Nor should you stand at the crossroads to cut off their fugitives, nor deliver up their survivors in the day of their distress’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Most scholars date the book shortly after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, because these verses match what other writings of that time say about Edom. A psalm remembers the Edomites calling for the city to be torn down to its foundations, and Lamentations and Ezekiel condemn Edom for its part in Judah's ruin. A minority date the book to the reign of Jehoram of Judah, about 848 to 841 BC, when Edom rebelled and Philistines and Arabs plundered Jerusalem. This site takes no side.

The verses move step by step from standing by to joining in. In the ancient world treaties between peoples were often called brotherhood, and real kinship carried a duty of protection. Casting lots for a captured city was how victors divided its goods and its people. Standing at the crossroads meant guarding the escape routes to catch the refugees fleeing the burning city and hand them over to the conquerors.

The word day sounds again and again: the day of misfortune, of destruction, of distress, of disaster. The prophet will not let Edom forget which day it was.
passages.later: A psalm remembers ‘the sons of Edom on the day Jerusalem fell’ (Psalm 137:7). Ezekiel also condemned Edom for its revenge on Judah (Ezekiel 25:12-14), and Edom's rebellion under Jehoram is told in 2 Kings 8:20-22.
passages.asks: Edom's first wrong was standing aside. Ask whose worst day you have watched from a distance. And ask whether you have ever gained anything from someone else's ruin.

passages.t: The Day of the LORD, and the kingdom
passages.happening:
‘For the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations. As you have done, it will be done to you; your recompense will return upon your own head’ (verse 15). As Edom drank on God's holy mountain, so the nations will drink the cup of judgment (verse 16).

‘But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, and it will be holy’ (verse 17), and the house of Jacob will take back its possession. The house of Jacob will be a fire and the house of Esau stubble (verse 18). People from the Negev, the foothills and Benjamin will possess the lands around them, and the exiles will come home as far as Zarephath and the towns of the Negev (verses 19-20). ‘The deliverers will ascend Mount Zion to rule over the mountains of Esau. And the kingdom will belong to the LORD’ (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The book widens from Edom to every nation. The Day of the LORD is near for all of them, and the rule is plain: what you do comes back on your own head. The punishment matches the crime: the looter is looted, and those who drank on God's holy mountain will drink the cup of judgment.

The last verses turn to the people who had lost everything. Deliverance will come on Mount Zion, and the exiles will return. Zarephath was a town belonging to Sidon, where Elijah once stayed (1 Kings 17:9). Sepharad, where some of Jerusalem's exiles lived, is named nowhere else in the Bible.

Edom's own decline followed within a century or two. By the time of Malachi its land lay waste, and Edomites had moved into southern Judah, later called Idumea. The final line is the point of the whole book: not that Judah wins, but that the kingdom belongs to the LORD.
passages.later: Malachi speaks of Edom's land laid waste (Malachi 1:2-4). Amos had promised that the house of David would possess ‘the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear My name’ (Amos 9:12).
passages.hard:
Is Obadiah simply a nationalist cry for revenge against Israel's rival?

Some readers find Obadiah uncomfortable because it rejoices in the fall of another people. Several things help. The charge is specific and moral: violence against a brother, looting, gloating, and handing refugees over to their killers. The vengeance belongs to God, not to Judah's armies, and it follows a rule of just repayment that applies to Israel too; Amos, just before Obadiah, condemned Israel for the same kinds of sin. And the horizon is wider than Edom: the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and the book ends with God's kingship, not Judah's.

Some interpreters still feel the tension between Obadiah's tone and Jesus' command to love enemies, and read the book as the honest cry of victims placed in God's hands rather than a model for revenge. Others see it as a needed word that God does not ignore atrocities.

Edom here is a real people of the ancient world. The book is not a code for any modern nation. It gives no warrant for hatred of, or violence against, any people today, and its promises about land make no claim about any modern state or border.
passages.asks: The book ends with the kingdom belonging to the LORD. Ask what difference it makes to a wronged person to leave judgment in God's hands. And ask what it would mean for your own life to belong to his kingdom, and not only to your side.
